'''John Peoples Jr.''' (January 22, 1933 – June 25, 2025) was an American physicist who served as [[Fermilab]]'s third director, served as director of the [[Sloan Digital Sky Survey]], and oversaw the shutdown of the [[Superconducting Super Collider]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Butler |first=Joel |last2=Holmes |first2=Stephen |date=2025-11-07 |title=John Peoples 1933–2025 |url=https://cerncourier.com/john-peoples-1933-2025/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=CERN Courier |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
John Peoples Jr. was born in New York City on January 22, 1933.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 1, 2008 |title=John Peoples, Jr. |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/K3099117596/BIC?u=wikipedia&sid=bookmark-BIC&xid=0454c739 |url-access=subscription |access-date=September 3, 2025 |website=Gale in Context: Biography}}</ref> After graduating from [[Staten Island Academy]] in 1950,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.statenislandacademy.org/giving/alumni/distinguished-graduates |title=Distinguished Graduates |publisher=[[Staten Island Academy]] |accessdate=February 1, 2019}}</ref> he received a BSEE from the [[Carnegie Mellon University|Carnegie Institute of Technology]] in 1955. He worked as an engineer at Martin-Marietta Corporation until 1959, when he entered [[Columbia University]].

==Research and teaching==
Peoples received his PhD in [[physics]] in 1966 and remained at Columbia as assistant professor of physics until 1969, when he began teaching at [[Cornell University]].<ref name="ACAP">{{cite web |url = https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?peoplesj/ |title = Array of Contemporary American Physicists: John Peoples Jr. |publisher = American Institute of Physics |accessdate= May 25, 2016 }}</ref>

==Career at Fermilab==
Peoples joined Fermilab as a physicist in 1971,<ref name="ACAP"/> eventually becoming head of the Proton Area<ref name="Fermilab book">{{cite book |last=Hoddeson |first=Lillian|authorlink=Lillian Hoddeson |last2=Kolb |first2=Adrienne|author2-link=Adrienne Kolb |last3=Westfall |first3=Catherine|author3-link=Catherine Westfall |date=2008 |title=Fermilab: Physics, the Frontier, and Megascience |location=Chicago, IL |publisher=University of Chicago Press |page=172 |isbn=978-0-226-34624-3}}</ref> and head of the Research Division in 1975.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Goldsborough |first=Bob |date=2025-07-25 |title=John Peoples, Fermilab director at time of top quark discovery, dies |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/07/25/john-peoples-fermilab-director-at-time-of-top-quark-discovery-dies/ |access-date=2025-07-28 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1981, Peoples became project manager of Tevatron I, which transformed the [[Tevatron]] from a fixed target accelerator to a proton-antiproton collider, and oversaw the construction of the Antiproton Source.<ref name="APS-DPF">{{cite web |url = https://www.aps.org/units/dpf/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=John&last_nm=Peoples&year=2010 |title = 2010 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators Recipient |publisher = American Physical Society |accessdate= May 25, 2016 }}</ref> Peoples left Fermilab briefly from 1987 to 1988 to assist the Central Design Group for the [[Superconducting Super Collider]] at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory]]. When he returned to Fermilab in the fall of 1988, he became deputy director of the lab. After [[Leon M. Lederman]] stepped down from the Fermilab directorship, Peoples became director on July 1, 1989.<ref name="Fermilab Archives Peoples bio">{{cite web |url = http://history.fnal.gov/jbio.html |title = John Peoples, Jr. |publisher = Fermilab |accessdate = May 25, 2016 |archive-date = May 23, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160523213631/http://history.fnal.gov/jbio.html |url-status = dead }}</ref>

During Peoples's time as Fermilab's director, the lab increased the Tevatron's luminosity by a factor of 20 between 1990 and 1994, which made it possible for Fermilab's experiments [[Collider Detector at Fermilab|CDF]] and [[D0 experiment|D0]] to discover the [[top quark]]. He also oversaw the construction of Fermilab's Main Injector from proposal in 1990 to completion in 1999, expanded the lab's work in experimental astrophysics, and modernized the lab's computing infrastructure to ensure it could handle the increasing demands of high-energy physics data. He stepped down from his position as Fermilab director in June 1999.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="APS-DPF" />

==Other positions==
In addition to his work at Fermilab, Peoples managed the shutdown of Superconducting Super Collider between 1993 and 1994, served as chairman of the International Committee for Future Accelerators, a working group of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]], from 1993 to 1997,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Membership {{!}} ICFA |url=https://icfa.hep.net/membership/ |access-date=2025-01-17 |language=en-US}}</ref> and was director of the [[Sloan Digital Sky Survey]] from June 1998 to June 2003. He stepped down from his position as Fermilab director in June 1999<ref name="Fermilab Archives Peoples bio" /> and retired from the lab in 2005. From 2003 to 2010, he served as director of the [[Dark Energy Survey]].<ref name=":0" /> The [[American Physical Society]] awarded him the [[Robert R. Wilson Prize|Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators]] in 2010.<ref name=":0" />

==Death==
Peoples died on June 25, 2025, in [[Bartlett, Illinois]], at the age of 92.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date= |title=Fermilab mourns the passing of John Peoples, third director |url=https://news.fnal.gov/2025/06/fermilab-mourns-the-passing-of-john-peoples-third-director |access-date=2025-07-04 |website=Fermilab |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0" />
